Hooded Oriole shows a crisp boundary between the black throat and the orange lower breast.

Hooded Oriole shows a narrow, pointed lower mandible and upper mandible suited to a probing bill shape.
Hooded Oriole has a tail that appears moderately long and slightly rounded at the tip.

Hooded Oriole shows orange flanks that match the belly rather than turning yellow or chestnut.
Hooded Oriole has underpart color that stays bright and fairly even from chest to vent.
Hooded Oriole shows a sleek neck and small head that enhance the long-billed profile.
Hooded Oriole has a black upper chest centered below the bill, forming a bib rather than a full black hood.
Hooded Oriole shows stronger contrast between its orange body and black wings than Orchard Oriole typically does.
Hooded Oriole has a finer, more tapered bill than the shorter straighter bill of Baltimore Oriole.
Hooded Oriole shows two narrow white wing bars instead of a single bold wing patch.

Nighthawk shows wing tips that are sharply pointed rather than broad and rounded.
Nighthawk has short legs that are usually inconspicuous beneath the body.
Nighthawk has plumage on the flanks marked with irregular dark bars and buff spotting.

Nighthawk has primaries that form the longest part of the wing silhouette.
Nighthawk shows a dark, fine bill that barely projects beyond the feathers of the face.
Nighthawk has an overall cryptic gray-brown palette rather than the stark monochrome of a raven.
Nighthawk shows subtle barring on the tail feathers in addition to the slight notch.
Nighthawk has a broad-based mouth line that reaches far back beneath the large eye.

Nighthawk shows buffy and dark patterning on the breast that merges gradually into the belly bars.

Brown Pelican has a massive lower mandible supporting the obvious pouch.

Brown Pelican shows a large pouch outline even when the bill is closed.

Brown Pelican has dark wings and body paired with a pale head, a combination not shown by frigatebirds.

White Pelican has a bulky body and a very large overall size.
White Pelican has long broad wings rather than the narrower pointed wings of gulls.
White Pelican has a long neck that appears thick and substantial.

White Pelican has a massive front-heavy silhouette created by the bill and pouch.
White Pelican has wings that appear wide and planklike because of its great size.
White Pelican has black wing tips that stand out strongly against otherwise white wings.
White Pelican has a tail that is plain pale rather than boldly patterned.
White Pelican has a thick neck merging into a deep-chested body.
White Pelican has an all-white body unlike Western Gull and California Gull, which show gray upperparts.
White Pelican has a uniformly pale neck and breast instead of the brown-toned foreparts of Brown Pelican.
White Pelican has a bill color that is usually pale yellowish rather than dark or sharply patterned.
White Pelican has a head profile dominated by the long straight bill rather than a rounded forehead alone.
White Pelican has underwings that are mostly white with black restricted to the flight feathers.
White Pelican has upperwings that look white across the coverts with black along the outer feathers.
White Pelican has a deeper body and thicker proportions than the slimmer gulls.
White Pelican has a clean white rump that continues the pale body color.
White Pelican has little body streaking or mottling compared with the darker mixed tones of Brown Pelican.
White Pelican has a very large pale pouch that forms a conspicuous arc under the bill.
White Pelican has a strong black-and-white wing pattern rather than the mostly uniform gray wings of gulls.

Whip poor Will shows wing coverts marked with fine mottled barring rather than a single bright patch.
Whip poor Will has a compact nightjar profile with pointed wings and a long narrow tail.
Whip poor Will shows a pale chin and upper throat standing out against darker bordering feathers.
Whip poor Will has belly markings that continue the barred and mottled pattern instead of turning plain.
Whip poor Will shows plumage tones that are mostly earthy brown and gray rather than olive and yellow.

Western Wood Pewee lacks the rich rufous or buffy wash on the lower belly typical of some Sayornis species.

Western Wood Pewee shows a restrained contrast between upperparts and underparts, giving an overall plain appearance.

Western Wood Pewee has a subdued gray-olive breast band effect rather than a sharply marked bib.
Western Wood Pewee has an overall dusky bill coloration that keeps the face from looking bright or colorful.
Western Wood Pewee shows a plain grayish chin and throat with little contrast against the rest of the head.
Western Wood Pewee has shoulder and scapular feathers that blend smoothly with the back, without bold paneling.
Western Wood Pewee appears more elongated and less tiny than Least Flycatcher because of its longer body and wings.

Common Raven: Common Raven is entirely glossy black from head to tail with no pale patches anywhere in the plumage.

Common Raven has broad wings with long fingered primary tips at the outer wing.
Common Raven shows a massive bill base that rises high onto the forehead, giving the face a heavy profile.
Common Raven has black head feathers with a glossy sheen rather than any contrasting crown or face pattern.
Common Raven has black upperparts across the back and mantle without streaking or spotting.
Common Raven has black underparts across the breast and belly with no pale belly or chest markings.
Common Raven has black wings both above and below, without white panels or pale flashes.
Common Raven has a black tail that is broad at the base and narrows toward the tip.

Common Raven shows a bulkier chest and deeper body than the slimmer crows.
Common Raven has a stout straight to slightly decurved bill rather than a slim delicate one.
Common Raven has thick black legs and feet matching the rest of the dark plumage.
Common Raven shows plain non-streaked body plumage with no bars, scalloping, or speckles.

Common Raven has black flight feathers that maintain an all-dark wing from shoulder to wingtip.

Common Raven has a deeper chest and thicker neck contour than the smaller Fish Crow.

Common Raven shows black ear coverts and sides of the head that blend smoothly into the neck.

Common Raven has a broad-based tail whose outer feathers are shorter than the central feathers, creating the wedge shape.
Common Raven shows long broad wings that suit its larger overall size among the confusable corvids.
Common Raven has a distinctly thick throat area because of the loose hackled feathers below the bill.
Common Raven has a more powerful-looking bill tip and deeper lower mandible than American Crow or Fish Crow.
Common Raven shows no white in the wings, tail, or body, separating it from Clark Nutcracker.
Common Raven has a larger and more imposing overall frame than any of the crow siblings in this task.
Common Raven has glossy black flanks and undertail area with no pale vent or undertail patches.
Common Raven shows a plain black rump and upper tail coverts continuous with the back.
Common Raven has dark eyes set in an all-black face, lacking any bold eye ring or facial marking.
Common Raven has broad rounded inner wings combined with splayed primary fingers at the tips.

Common Raven has all-black plumage with an oily purple-blue gloss in good light, but no contrasting white areas.
